Su Blackwell Enchants with Folkloric Stories That Spring from Vintage Books
The artist's new exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us.

From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled Pathway of Crumbs , draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.

Nodding to the enduring children’s story of Hansel and Gretel , the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition.

Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.
Pathway of Crumbs is on view from November 25 to January 25 at Long & Ryle in London. Find more from Blackwell on her website .

This year's holiday ads have one thing in common, and it's good news for creatives
Michael Feder, founding partner at Hornet, assesses this year's batch of seasonal ads and identifies one overriding theme that unites them all. With Prada, Levi's and Dior all turning to…
Michael Feder, founding partner at Hornet, assesses this year's batch of seasonal ads and identifies one overriding theme that unites them all.

With Prada, Levi's and Dior all turning to animation for their festive spots, craft as a symbol for the holidays is stronger than ever. At the same time, convincing audiences of authentic craft is getting harder.

Dior is now facing backlash, with viewers debating how much AI played a role in creating its Marlene Dietrich-inspired spot. Director Sylvain Chomet has denied using generative AI in the project, though he has acknowledged the use of automated interpolation to generate some of the intermediate frames that make movement fluid.

It's an interesting—and welcome—development: the strength of reaction and scrutiny shows that people appreciate craft and are paying increasing attention to how content is created. They are becoming a kind of AI police, tired of shortcuts and craving care and authenticity in what brands serve up, especially when it comes to the magic of the holidays.

With discourse and changing sentiments around AI now making reactions to a holiday ad more complex, the thing that creatives can always come back to is the visible evidence that a real team made decisions and put thought, effort, and care into the final result.
1. The strongest work is built with humanity at its core.

This year’s La Mer holiday campaign shows how. Director Samuel Jerome Mason drew inspiration from mid-century stagecraft and classic holiday window displays, set in a theatrical, nostalgic CG world. Rather than simply showcasing the products, the campaign gives audiences a sense of nostalgia and artistry to admire, helping it have a human feel.
2. Restraint helps to cut through noise

The holidays are the most emotional time of year for audiences, making it an important moment to lean into sentiment and slowness. The most persuasive work has elements of restraint, particularly within the luxury industry, where quiet simplicity is emphasised. A useful test is whether the original founder or designer would recognise the work as their own. If the answer is no, it's probably too loud.

Looking to the past can help here, leaning into archival motifs or advertising. Intentional use of materials can also anchor a campaign in restraint rather than novelty, with embroidery, silk, and paper as useful symbols of luxury while maintaining craft.

Brands should focus on creating scalable worlds rather than one-off spots. The world can be used across films, stills, billboards and social assets, and be released in stages across the season. Take La Mer's 2025 campaign , which created an immersive world for products within an Art Deco, Great Gatsby-inspired party.

Similarly, the animated 'The Bear and the Hare' ad we made with Blinkink for John Lewis was accompanied by a hardback book and ebook, merchandise including toys and baby clothing, and a soundtrack by Lily Allen, which reached number one on the UK Singles Chart.

Although over 10 years old now, the world of 'The Bear and the Hare' can be revisited year after year, connected to a broader cultural conversation and emotional reaction. This makes the campaign become part of something bigger than simply a sales moment.
4. Brands need to be specific about the craft they choose

The craft alone is not the message: if every brand uses animation or celebrities to signal humanity, it diminishes the meaning. Brands should choose a format that makes sense for their category and be specific about why they chose that craft. For example, animation and luxury go hand in hand because animation shows the patience, attention to detail, and emotional response that has always been associated with luxury.

I appreciate that so many luxury brands are producing ads created by incredibly talented illustrators, animators, and individual artists this year. Rimowa's papercraft holiday campaign, created in collaboration with animation studio Studio Linguini, alongside creative agency GUT Amsterdam, stands out to me as smart and charming. Work like this promotes a sense of discovery for audiences, and an authentic connection to authorship.

It's all too easy to be cynical. In the digital age, whole online communities seem driven by bitterness and contrarianism. Enter Luke McConkey , a welcome antidote to these attitudes. His joyful illustrations are deliberately designed to cheer up viewers, because as he argues: "Smiles are infectious; they take a small amount of effort on your part but spread like wildfire."

Luke's journey to becoming an upbeat artist is built on a childhood love of drawing, spending afternoons poring over How to Draw Comics the Marvel Way before showing off what he learnt in school the next week. As with lots of creatives though, this passion was temporarily shelved in favour of more traditional subjects like IT and history.

"I still had a love for drawing, but it was a hobby which then got pushed further down the pecking order when I discovered music, video games, going out with mates and stuff like that," he tells Creative Boom. "It was, however, always there in the back of my mind."

Upon graduating from an Interactive Media Design course at LJMU, Luke landed himself a job at a design agency. Over the course of six years, he worked his way up to become a lead designer, focusing on logo design and visual identity. "Aaron Draplin was huge for me in those years around 2016."

In 2017, he took the plunge and became a freelance graphic designer, but it soon dawned on him that creative, illustrative vignettes were what he enjoyed most. As the pandemic rumbled on in 2020 through to 2021, Luke decided to pivot into being purely an illustrator.

"I started drawing and drawing, making images in different styles, and slowly got something which resembles my current illustration style, and just kept at it," he says. "I didn't want the process to get in the way; I wanted it to be muscle memory so that I could just create.

"I took a course with InkyGoodness to try and help build a portfolio and learn about the industry. This led me to realise what an illustration agent was, and in 2022 I took the punt of all punts and approached Handsome Frank to see if they'd rep me…it took a little convincing (which is a story of its own!), but they did!"

Speaking of his style, it's fair to say that joy is the common ingredient found in all of Luke's work. He puts this down to being a positive person overall. "I really like the idea of spreading joy; I think it's something you need to consciously work on," he says.

"It's very easy to succumb to being sad, angry, down, and we all love a moan, don't we? That is important, but it's hard to find good things, make people smile, or celebrate. I always like to think if my work can put a smile on someone's face, then it's a job well done."

Of course, this means Luke sometimes has to force the positive vibes, but it's a role he's more than happy to take on. "I'm also of an age where I am not really too fussed about what people think, so being a little silly, goofy, having fun and embarrassing is fine," he adds.

"If we really want to get into it, get existential, life's mad, isn't it? We're floating on a blue orb, our lives are mere specks on the cosmic landscape, and relatively no one will remember when you sang Karaoke badly in 100 years, so go, do it, have fun and don't give a fuck."

Why are football clubs launching Christmas campaigns (and do John Lewis and M&S have anything to worry about?)
Chelsea, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City have all gone big for Christmas this year. So what have they created, and why? When I was an eight-year-old boy, clutching my 50p ticket…
Chelsea, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City have all gone big for Christmas this year. So what have they created, and why?

When I was an eight-year-old boy, clutching my 50p ticket every Saturday to Bristol City FC's juvenile enclosure, the world was very different. Back then, a club's idea of a Christmas campaign was a team photo in Santa hats in the match programme. Well, those days seem to be long gone.

In the 2020s, big teams launch their festive campaigns in early November, around the same time as supermarkets and department stores. And just like with John Lewis and M&S, you can expect celebrity cameos, out-of-home campaigns and big-name agency credits to match.

This year, four of the Premier League's heavyweights have gone out to make a big old Christmas splash. Chelsea has built a fake TV network. Liverpool has turned its Christmas message into a thank-you note. Arsenal has hired Colin Firth. And Manchester City has handed the pens to local schoolchildren.
Let's look at each in turn, and then have a think about what this means for the culture in general.

This year, Chelsea looked at the idea of a single Christmas ad up and down, made a face, and thought: "Nah, we can do better than that". Instead, the club has turned itself into an entire festive TV network, complete with its own weather forecast, phone-in, shopping channel and ad breaks, all selling the club's Christmas range.

Sports broadcaster Jolie Sharpe sells the range, QVC-style. TalkSport presenter Jason Cundy brings radio phone-in mayhem. Striker João Pedro answers fans in Ask João, and fellow team member Cole Palmer delivers the weather "as cold as ever". Other players from across the men's and women's squads, including Levi Colwill, Katie McCabe, Ellie Carpenter and Alyssa Thompson, also get involved.

The rollout of the campaign, created by agency Till Dawn with strategy from consultancy Iconic, has been epic. Fans got the outtakes first: fourth-wall breaks, asides to camera and players corpsing. Then came the channels, scattered across different platforms, and only at the end does the full programme arrive.

"Fans watch football flicking between clips, streams, reactions and live shopping within the same phone, so this Christmas Chelsea broadcasts everywhere all at once," explains James Kirkham, founder of Iconic. "You find it in pieces, channel-hop your way through a different clip or show on every platform, and it brings back that can't-wait wanting of circling the Christmas catalogue, before it all turned into cardboard boxes on the doorstep."
"We shot it like a live network with every camera rolling, so the corpsing, the asides and the looks off to the AD are as much the show as the show," adds Till Dawn founder Craig Stronach.
A percentage of sales from the festive range goes to Chelsea Foundation and its charity partners to tackle loneliness and social isolation across London.

While Chelsea has gone all-out this Christmas, Liverpool has kept things simpler, with a single message. Rather than sell anything up front, it uses its traditional Christmas spot to thank fans, in the most Scouse way possible: "Nice one."
In the hero film, Dear Reds, players from the men's and women's teams, including Virgil van Dijk, Alexis Mac Allister, Alisson Becker, Florian Wirtz and Grace Fisk, thank supporters directly.

Their words play over photos and footage of fans from Merseyside and around the world, much of it user-generated. It ends with the line: "This club doesn't belong to us. But we're honoured to represent it. And it's an honour to play for you. To the world's greatest fans, nice one."

Out-of-home ads are appearing near Official Liverpool Supporters Club locations in 24 cities across 16 countries and five continents, from Dublin and Oslo to Bangkok, Jakarta and Cape Town. "With 'Nice One', we're putting the world's greatest fans at the heart of our Christmas campaign and delivering football's biggest-ever thank you to the people who help make this club so special," says Hannah Pym, senior vice president of marketing and digital at Liverpool FC.

Helen Bur’s Monumental Bordeaux Mural Celebrates Motherhood and Female Solidarity, France
British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.

Elegance Flows Through Sheena Liam’s Embroideries in Green

Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness . Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.
The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram .

Susitse’s lifelong interest in canids didn’t just push the Finnish illustrator, comic artist and graphic designer also known as Essi Välimäki to refine her creative skills. Ιt was a springboard to seek self-knowledge and perfect the art of self-expression. Her striking, colour-saturated illustrations look straight into the mouth of the beast and expose its heart — inner demons, low self-esteem, toxic relationships, overthinking, grief. A life spent on autopilot.

A time of mental health struggles and targeted self-reflection drove Susitse to find an outlet and seek out people on social media that would help her feel less alone with her emotions, sharing personal messages wrapped in feral snarls of creativity.

Susitse’s surreal, spectacular beasts have human features that convey a touching vulnerability, paired with insightful writing that gives voice to troubled souls everywhere. In her creations, horror and savage comics intertwine with the fragility of human expression, her very real life challenges transforming into dark fables of discovery and self-acceptance. They are lessons in survival and hope exploding in colour — ferocious reds, fantastical purples and luminous yellows.

A daily routine dictated by an employer is, in fact, what inspired Susitse’s prize-winning, poignantly resonant work, Autopilot , kicking back against the idea that we are only meant to be useful cogs in a machine. Playfully dotted with analogue imagery, a multi-headed wolf growls with the age-old fear that our value is limited to performance and production. It is a downright liberating achievement coming from Susitse’s current place as a full-time working artist; a captivating, deeply resonant howl for freedom.
You’ve touched a chord with people online through your illustrations and writing. Does this kind of honest expression come naturally to you, or is it something you have to work on?

Yes, my artistic work has managed to touch people’s hearts all around the world, and I am deeply grateful and humbled to have been able to help people through my art. Open expression comes naturally to me, and it’s reflected both in my art and in my life. I believe that even difficult emotions should not be something to hide or feel ashamed of. Emotions, whether positive or negative, all exist as equals.

This is why I have many unfinished works, as ideas come to me faster than I can actually execute them!

That said, every piece begins with an idea, followed by a quick sketch to plan the composition and colour palette. Next comes the line art phase, followed by base colouring, where the piece receives its initial foundation colours. After that, I determine the direction of the light source and proceed to add shadows and highlights. There is something about Andrada Trapnell’s paintings that feels strangely familiar, as though you’ve encountered these moments somewhere before, tucked away in the recesses of your memory, only to have them suddenly return. Looking at her work is a little like reaching inside a jewelry box and pulling out a charm you haven’t seen in years. For a moment, you’re transported. A feeling rushes over you, a memory begins to take shape, and yet you’re not entirely certain where it belongs. Was it something you experienced? Something you dreamed? Or is it a moment that exists somewhere between the two, in liminal spaces?

Her paintings feel like tucked-away worlds, each one waiting to be discovered. And there’s something so intriguing about the way the recurring circles invite you to experience them. From the outside, you might take in the painting as a whole, following its colors, patterns, and abstract forms. But the circle seems to offer another way in. One Saliva Bubble: How David Lynch tried to go mainstream
"So, she said to him 'poo-poo on your pee-pee'!"

Considered by many to be the greatest piece of television ever made, Twin Peaks: The Return was a seismic moment even to die-hard fans of David Lynch because it proved one thing that no one saw coming.
His entire career before it had been him holding back.

Yes, baffling movies like Inland Empire , Eraserhead and Mulholland Drive had been Lynch not necessarily on easy mode, but definitely trying to curb some of his more esoteric traits and make his signature style more accessible to others. On the one hand, this is just as well. Twin Peaks: The Return left several people who weren’t high-minded TV critics baffled, confused and bored.

On the other hand, it does ask a tantalising question. What if Lynch tried to actively talk down to his audience and open himself up to making a full-on blockbuster? While his most accessible work, The Straight Story , is also his most low-key and low-stakes, it remains his biggest attempt at a blockbuster alongside Dune . His sole attempt at an adaptation, and one that still alienated several people for all the wrong reasons. What was Lynch’s idea of a film to get butts in seats?

Well, we actually have some idea thanks to his work in the aftermath of Dune . He was in dire straits after that film died a horrible death at the box office, and he was very lucky to get a gritty, somewhat grotesque crime thriller like Blue Velvet off the ground afterwards even at its tiny budget compared to the heights of Dune . Thus, after the success of that film steadied the ship, Lynch was paired with Hill Street Blues showrunner Mark Frost to begin work on the script of his next project.

After the duo initially began work on a shelved Marilyn Monroe biopic, they started work on their idea of a surefire hit, which became One Saliva Bubble . This is a script which really is levelled at the lowest common denominator at points. If you need an example, the inciting incident of the entire film involves a security guard at a military complex saying, “So, she said to him ‘poo-poo on your pee-pee!'”, and laughing so hard that he spits the titular bubble onto a console he’s guarding.

This causes a short circuit in a satellite it’s controlling, which then makes it shoot a laser beam onto a small town in Kansas, causing all of its inhabitants to swap bodies at random. This led to 90 minutes of slapstick fun built around a family man swapping bodies with a psychotic hitman, that Lynch himself described as “out-and-out wacko, dumb comedy”. To be clear, he wasn’t being entirely snooty about this, he said that he and Frost essentially spent the entire writing process thinking of things about the body swap premise that made them laugh and just crammed them into the script one after the other.
Considering they had just finished making Blue Velvet , I can imagine this was a refreshing change of pace.

What’s more, the script was a massive deal in Hollywood. Everyone who read it loved it and was willing to give Lynch a chance after a flop like Dune and a grim little thriller like Blue Velvet could have made him radioactive. Martin Short and Steve Martin signed up to star in the picture; all was set for work on One Saliva Bubble to begin. However, this was when Lynch still had a contract with Dino De Laurentiis’ production company, and six weeks before shooting was due to start, the company filed for bankruptcy.

What brings this full circle, though, is what Lynch and Frost did next. After two Hollywood projects in a row that stalled despite them not only working well together, but enjoying it too, their shared agent suggested they find a project that could work in Frost’s native medium of TV. Frost and Lynch went to a coffee shop in Los Angeles and started work on an idea that would combine the small-town absurdity and broad comedy of One Saliva Bubble with the crime thriller grit of Blue Velvet .
They came away with the pitch, premise and series outline for a little show called Twin Peaks . Not bad for a knucklehead comedy, right?

Daniel Zvereff, director of the new animated feature Moonfish , carefully considers the role science fiction should play in this current moment.

When I was a child, I’d lie in the yard at night, stare at the sky and dream about leaving Earth. My head was full of the rings of Saturn and the red dust of Mars, thinking about worlds where nobody had ever walked. The Apollo missions, the Soviet cosmonauts, the disasters and the triumphs: back then, it felt like proof that no matter how ugly geopolitics got down here, curiosity could still pull us forward together.

Maybe that was a child’s delusion, but our collective relationship with space has since changed into something almost unrecognizable. Over the past 20 years, space has become privatized. If you watch a commercial rocket launch today, the aesthetic is slick: carbon-fiber hulls, tablet consoles and bespoke spacesuits tailored to look good on social media feeds. Private capital sells off-planet travel like a venture-backed manifest destiny, an escape hatch for a ruined planet bought with tech fortunes. Billionaires pay for three minutes of zero gravity, holding up flowers in orbit for multi-camera livestreams cut like fashion commercials. Hollywood mostly plays along. Modern sci-fi gives us clean, digital environments where the actual misery of the void gets buried under good lighting and industrial chic. Characters fly pristine ships, solving crises through sheer heroic grit. It looks great on screen, but it ignores how human labor actually works on a frontier.

Every time people pushed into extreme environments to dig up resources, whether it was on Pacific whaling ships, North Sea oil platforms or in boomtown mines, the story was never about freedom. It was about exploitation: impossible quotas, broken bodies and deadening isolation. Right now, in the new digital frontier, data centers are chewing through power grids and overheating the planet to run algorithmic models. I am very much a homebird, so when it came time for Manic Street Preachers to go on tour I was nervous about it. My Dad had an old grandad’s chair, which he managed to tie to the wall in the back of the hire van, so someone could have a seat on the way to the gig. It was incredibly dangerous. We had such a deep bonding experience on the Motown Junk Tour in 1991. The staff at the venues were just so friendly; you felt that they really cared. I remember getting to the Stoke Wheatsheaf – a magical venue – and we hadn’t had any food for a day and a half. They made us the most beautiful burger and chips.

King Tut’s Wah Wah Hut, Glasgow? The Stoker, Coventry? The Barrel Organ, Birmingham? JB’s, Dudley? Moles, Bath? The Adelphi, Hull? The Leadmill, Sheffield? It was a truly magical tour, I can’t even remember any bad shows.

The greatest one was probably The Buzz Club in Aldershot. What a fucking venue. Who’d have thought if you were in a rock band, going to Aldershot would give you one of the greatest gigs of your life? It was full of squaddies because it’s an army town, and it was antagonistic, but also brilliant. That was on the edge but some gigs could tip over the edge.

We did quite a scary gig at Reading’s After Dark Club. There was a proper firm of football hooligans there. There was a real adrenaline rush to it, even if there was a hint of violence at a lot of those early gigs.

What strikes me now is that all of these places were towns and I wonder how many of them have that kind of gig venue left. You can still play gigs in the cities, but to play in these towns was amazing: learning your trade and meeting people. Also realising there are people like you in every town you go to.

Very early doors, Little Chefs were different – they deserve an honourable mention because you could just get a proper meal there. A plate of bacon, egg and chips. We loved going to them but even by the time we started touring they were getting harder to find. And in the services before they improved, all you could find was some dodgy pasty that had been sitting in a fridge for weeks. But I have a theory that bad food equals great music. Show me a band that’s eaten healthy food all of their lives and their music is always shit. Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits First Love in Video for “Hush Now” — “Trip” EP Out Now!
Here we are again You look so familiar In this red light… Drop your mask, my friend Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and… The post Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits…

Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and bring back every little thing you did to look at ease. You remember where you put your hands and the joke you made while you worked up the nerve to ask them to stay. The relief came when they heard the question in the joke and stayed a little longer. It can take years to realize how much you miss being known that well.

At the opening of “Hush Now (The Calling),” Apolonia sings to a familiar face bathed in red light, as king them to drop the mask with the gentle insistence of an old friend inviting you to sit and stay awhile. The track is the lead single from Trip , the four-track EP released November 20 by Hamburg noise-pop trio Seasurfer .

Christian Klepp ’s footage casts the first verse’s red light across the stage. Red and yellow projections sweep the back wall, while green glints in the dark glasses above a ribbed microphone. Maysterwerke cuts from this intimate close-up to wider shots, where amber haze reduces the band to little more than silhouettes.
Watch the video for Hush Now (The Calling) below.

The way the band moves in and out of view has a counterpart in the arrangements Dirk Knight began imagining in New York. “For me, this is the sound of cities,” says the instrumentalist, who recorded, produced and mixed the EP. He keeps the bass and drums fairly still while the guitars and the voices of Apolonia and Kiora drift in and out of focus.

Those guitars have been a constant since Seasurfer’s first two albums on Saint Marie Records and through collaborations with Cocteau Twins’ Robin Guthrie and producer John Fryer. This year the band put them to work on the post-punk of June’s Angels , then let them fill the room on August’s shoegaze-heavy The Noise is ours . On their third EP of 2026, a trip-hop beat gives the guitar chords more room to ring.

You can hear that space in the first bars of the opening track , One . The guitars drone and the drums take their time, leaving room for the strings that Chandeen’s Harald Löwy adds to the arrangement. The higher voices blur into the chords the way they do on My Bloody Valentine’s Loveless . The low lead comes through with the intimacy of someone speaking in confidence. It’s a seductive way to sing about making peace with your own company and the knowledge that we come and go alone.
Watch the video for One, filmed by Ahmed Sarowar and edited by Dirk Knight, below:

That intimacy carries into Hush Now (The Calling) , where a sigh of synths stretches into long, luminous lines and Knight’s guitars bring warmth up from below. Apolonia and Kiora’s voices cascade through the chorus, opening the melody out the way Elizabeth Fraser could on Cocteau Twins’ Heaven or Las Vegas and Milk & Kisses . Apolonia describes the song as a memory of first love, and Kiora hears loss and longing in the words. When the refrain comes round to “I’m by your side,” the reassurance sounds as necessary to the person giving it as it does to the one hearing it.

The guitar comes further forward on “Disappear” , where the opening loop has the woozy repetition of Cocteau Twins’ Otherness EP. The voice has Cranes’ reserve and some of Portishead’s unease. When the drums drop away, the guitar keeps circling long enough for you to stop anticipating the next hit. By the time it comes, the loop has built up a charge that carries into the closing bars.

The drums make you wait for them again on “I See You” . The guitars pile up first, with the soft-edged distortion of Loveless , and the drum machine gives them a trip-hop lilt when it comes in. There’s some of Cranes’ distance in the singing and some of the poise of Siobhan de Maré on Mono’s “Life in Mono.” At under three minutes, the closer rewards a second pass. Follow a guitar you barely noticed the first time through, and you can hear the arrangement shift around it.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? , sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam ‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

What does access look like for disabled gig goers in 2026?
The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig

Attitude is Everything connects disabled people with music and live event industries, to improve access together. Starting in 2000, the charity has supported industry pros and organisations to help better understand and improve access for Deaf, disabled and neurodivergent people in music.

The charity’s State of Access Report - a report set up to set standards for national progress with disability in music - lays out exactly what that looks like in 2026, and how fraught with problems it can be, alongside the scale of the extra burden it places on disabled fans so they can safely enjoy their night out.
It’s the first report in eight years, and the first since Covid-19. In that time, the volume of the conversation around access in live music has hit a fever pitch.
It's partly out of necessity, given that Covid-19 has been described as a "mass disabling event", and as of 2023, 2 million people in the UK are estimated to be living with long Covid.

This fan-led review echoes similar calls to improve inclusion across music events. 24% of Music Fans Voice respondents disagreed (compared to 58% who agreed) with the statement that live music events currently reflect the demographic diversity of the UK.
There's a disability tax on attending live gigs

The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig, the most common of which (66%) relates to travel or accommodation. Other common access related costs include health or recovery costs (40%), personal assistant or companion costs (28%), higher ticket prices (25%) or food and drink for medical purposes (23%). Sadly, 58% of fans say extra costs have stopped them from attending an event.

The most frequent barrier disabled fans encounter relates to poor or inaccurate access information, which 69.5% of fans say they've experienced. Meanwhile, lack of seating or rest spaces is a barrier for 66.4% of respondents, booking or ticketing systems for 56.1% and staff attitudes or behaviour for 51.6%.
Access is inconsistent across the board

Only 20% of disabled gig goers say they feel they can consistently rely on their access needs being met. Even more starkly, 94% say they expose themselves to some level of risk when they go to a show.
The burden still falls on disabled people to advocate for themselves

72% of disabled gig goers have had to resolve access problems themselves, while 62% report having to explain their needs repeatedly. Just under half (48%) of respondents have said they've supported other disabled fans in the past, while more than half say they've had to leave events early due to access issues.
Fortunately, 58% of those surveyed said that they think access has improved in the last five years, and 61% would describe events as 'somewhat' or 'very' accessible.

"The findings from the survey are shocking, but sadly not surprising. But, by sharing the feedback with the sector, and supporting the music industry to embed access, we aim to improve the experiences for the disabled community, because by removing barriers, we don’t just open doors, we open up an entire industry."

These Holiday Cooking Mistakes Could Put Your Family’s Safety at Risk
The American Red Cross is advising Americans to follow these easy safety rules in the kitchen this holiday season.

The holidays are supposed to be about good food, time with loved ones and enjoying a little holiday tradition. But before everyone gathers around the table, there’s something to keep in mind: A few common cooking mistakes can put your family and home at risk.

The American Red Cross is reminding Americans to take extra precautions this holiday season, especially in the kitchen. After all, Thanksgiving Day is the leading day of the year for home cooking fires. With busy kitchens, multiple dishes cooking at once and distractions everywhere, it’s easy to overlook something that could become dangerous.
Simple Thanksgiving cooking habits can help prevent fires and hazards
It doesn’t take a major mistake for a fire to start. That’s what makes kitchen fires so sneaky and dangerous.
The Red Cross recommends staying in the kitchen whenever you’re using the stovetop or oven. If you need to step away, even briefly, turn off the appliance first.

Be careful about what you’re wearing, too. Loose clothing and dangling sleeves can easily catch fire. Likewise, items like paper towels, oven mitts, wooden utensils, food packaging and curtains should stay away from hot appliances.
If you have children or pets, the Red Cross says to establish a safe cooking zone. Keep them at least three feet away from cooking areas.
Also, be prepared. It’s a good idea to have a fire extinguisher nearby and know how to use it before an emergency happens.

Both Thanksgiving and Christmas often involve turkeys, so note that turkey fryers deserve extra attention. Anyone preparing a fried turkey should keep the fryer outdoors, away from the house, garage and other structures. It should sit on a flat, stable surface, and the turkey must be completely thawed before it goes into the fryer.
Aside from these tips, it’s also good to keep up with current recalls , so that what you’re serving at dinner is safe.
The Red Cross recommends downloading its free Red Cross Emergency app , which offers safety information and customizable weather alerts.
The holidays should be a time for making memories, not dealing with an emergency. A few smart moves in the kitchen can go a long way toward keeping everyone safe.

Joost Vandebrug explores how separate views and moments come to be seen as a whole. His landscapes gather fragments into places that feel familiar, even when no single place could contain them. The image takes shape through remembering and looking, while the joins keep its construction visible.

Each work is built from dozens of photo-emulsion transfers on handmade paper cards. I transfer and reassemble them individually. Nothing is ever the same — every card has its imperfections. When I lay them together, they form a new landscape — part remembered, part reinvented.

These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as The Night Watch , Girl with a Pearl Earring , and The Garden of Earthly Delights . But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the Ghent Altarpiece , also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb , by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching the video from The Gaze above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at the online Ghent Altarpiece , seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

But that may only stoke your desire to make a pilgrimage of your own, to Belgium, where you can see the real thing carefully placed in St. Bavo’s Cathedral. In the early fifteenth century, when that institution was called St. John the Baptist’s Church, its warden was the wealthy merchant Jodocus Vijd. Having endowed a new chapel, Vijd also commissioned the van Eyck brothers to create an altarpiece spectacular enough to secure him a spot in the afterlife. The result was one of the earliest masterpieces of oil painting.

Even apart from that designation (to say nothing of its being the most stolen work of art in history ), it has enjoyed an impressive afterlife of its own. Of the many who have traveled to behold it in situ at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecstasy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But others have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it beforehand, by all the attention the artists put into integrating the work with its surroundings. The light within its images, for example, is painted in such a way as to match the light streaming into the cathedral itself. Those who look closely at the gem worn by the foremost singing angel will see a reflection of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the knowing gaze of the sacrificial lamb, they’re all but guaranteed to have a religious experience — though whether its nature is Christian, artistic, or otherwise will depend, as it does with all enduring art, on the individual viewer.

What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture
And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It…

Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above .

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame ) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

A food studies scholar provides some tips for throwing the perfect Friendsgiving gathering.

One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.
While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.
If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.

Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity.

Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.

Mogging is the word of the year – but men have been doing it since Shakespearean times
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.
The Collins English Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year.

The Collins website says that the word originated with the acronym AMOG – or “alpha male of the group” – which is often associated with bodybuilding forums and, more recently, the toxic culture of incels and the manosphere . But mogging has now entered mainstream language with its meaning slightly repurposed: to describe someone who is outperforming, outshining or upstaging someone.

While the verb is often used in reference to physical looks, it can also be applied in other contexts. Alex Beecroft , managing director of Collins, explained that the selection of mogging demonstrates how “each generation leaves its mark on language”, with the term seeing a 210% increase in usage in 2026.
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.

The Oxford English Dictionary contains four historic meanings of the base verb “mog”. The earliest meaning and usage comes as early as 1674, referring to card games “to exchange a card with the dealer”. A later usage means “to move on, depart, decamp”. By the mid-1800s, two new possible meanings emerged : “to walk slowly but steadily” and “to shift (a person, animal etc.) to cause to move on (esp. quickly)”.

What unites these historic meanings is the connection to movement or performance. For many men in the early modern period, the demonstration of superiority through action and movement was a key method to showcase, or perhaps fittingly, “mog” others.

New research by theatre historian Eleanor Rycroft explores this link between movement, gender and social power. Rycroft examines theatrical works by playwrights such as Shakespeare and Ben Jonson alongside historical conduct books and household management guides, revealing just how much cultural capital was attached to a man’s posture and stride.

How-to guides and etiquette books from the time told men and women how to behave, labelling certain traits as respectable and others as improper. In the 1566 English translation of Ortensio Landi’s Delectable Demaundes and Pleasaunt Questions (1566), readers were shown how to outdo other men in wit and conduct. Yet in doing so, the text also exposed the cracks in this ideal, revealing how precarious that masculine status truly was.

In his influential Book of the Courtier (1528), courtier and diplomat Baldassare Castiglione defined this quality as a “certain nonchalance, which shall conceal design and show that what is done and said is done without effort and almost without thought”.
Sprezzatura in Shakespeare and asserting manhood
Castiglione was first translated into English by Sir Thomas Hoby in 1561, and the concept of sprezzatura heavily influenced early modern English culture.

In many early modern plays, characters demonstrate the importance of asserting a mastery of manhood and, with it, upstaging others. While Shakespeare does not use the terms sprezzatura or mogging in any of his works, many men attempt to outperform or outshine other characters to assert or affirm their manly status.

In Much Ado About Nothing (first performed 1598), the “merry war” between protagonists Beatrice and Benedick – a rapid-fire exchange loaded with insults as the two characters shield their true feelings for one another – is often a source of audience amusement and laughter. However, this “skirmish of wit” points to the different expectations on men and women for Benedick across the play text: to match and ideally best Beatrice’s skill in wordplay so as not to emasculate himself.

Beatrice seems to be aware of these dynamics of masculinity, noting that Benedick “gets nothing” from their verbal exchanges – after their last encounter, “four of his five wits went halting off, and now is the whole man governed with one”. These scenes of verbal sparring might be understood as a trial of masculinity, testing Benedick’s skills in rhetoric and wordplay.

East Germany exiled singer Wolf Biermann. They only made his message louder
Fifty years ago the GDR withdrew the citizenship of the prominent leftwing dissident. It turned him into an international symbol – and cemented his place in history

November 16 marks 50 years since one of the most notorious examples of artistic censorship from the 20th century: the East German government’s stripping the citizenship of dissident singer-songwriter Wolf Biermann .
Far from quashing Biermann’s voice, this act of political exile amplified it, and cemented his place in history, underscored by a new documentary about his life story.

It is a lesson others should have done more to heed. Earlier this year, US billionaire Robert Kraft and other stadium owners banned Macklemore from their venues over pro-Palestinian remarks the singer made during his support slot on Ed Sheeran’s tour.
But in trying to silence the rapper, Kraft and his cohort unintentionally amplified his message .
The story of Biermann can tell us much about how attempts to quash the political expression of musicians have spectacularly backfired.
From East German darling to dissident
Biermann, born in 1936, became a prominent figure within East German left-wing dissident artists and intellectuals in the late 1960s. But he wasn’t always an outsider.

As the West German immigrant son of a Jewish communist killed in Auschwitz, and a mentee of Bertolt Brecht, Biermann was initially the darling of the East German press, and held a candidate membership of the Socialist Unity Party (SED).

When his lyrics became critical of the SED, however, the Stasi (secret police) began a campaign of harassment that escalated over more than a decade. It included performance bans, sabotage, intimidation, round-the-clock surveillance, bugging, reports from more than 200 Stasi informants , and even a veiled death threat.
Yet this persecution amplified Biermann’s voice and gave him an international platform.
The making of an international symbol
Western governments adopted Biermann as a potent symbol in the cultural Cold War. He acquired famous fans, including Joan Baez and Allen Ginsberg.
Numerous organisations awarded him prizes. CBS gave him a record deal, and West Berlin radio stations frequently broadcast his music into East Germany.

These broadcasts made some remarkable converts. Gerulf Pannach, a young songwriter and then Stasi informant , first heard Biermann’s music while working as a border guard. He befriended the singer, renounced the Stasi and began writing his own critical lyrics.
Pannach convinced Christian Kunert, the keyboardist of the beloved rock band Renft , to take an anti-state position in 1974.

Kunert, in turn, introduced writer and social psychologist Jürgen Fuchs – who would go on to become a prominent East German dissident – to Pannach and Biermann. He also converted his Renft band mate Thomas “Monster” Schoppe to the cause.
Closer to home, Biermann’s former stepdaughter, young rock singer and future queen of punk Nina Hagen , introduced her bandmates to Biermann.

Biermann’s inner circle was, for a time, paradoxically protected by their fame as dissidents. Aided by Western media, they flouted state controls in ways average East Germans wouldn’t dare. While the state maintained tight surveillance of Biermann’s circle, they seemed hesitant to arrest them.
But those more loosely associated with Biermann often found themselves caught in the crossfire of multiple Stasi operations to harass and crush dissidents.
This included band members of Renft, who helped Pannach bypass his performance ban and perform Biermann’s songs, and publicly denounced East German border policy.
As a result, members of Renft were repeatedly summoned and questioned by the authorities. Then the band was banned. In September 1975, a local licensing board told Renft they “no longer exist”.
Taboo themes in Pannach’s lyrics were the pretext for the ban , but declassified Stasi documents suggest the state ultimately targeted them as proxies for Biermann.
The regime accidentally elevated a popular East German rock band to anti-state legends.

A further attempt to neutralise Renft through conscription and a tax investigation converted the band’s thus far apolitical founder, Klaus Jentzsch, into a gifted anti-state organiser. With Biermann’s help, he coordinated a transnational multi-media campaign.

Trash-hungry robots roam Japan’s busiest train station
The colorful, googly-eyed robots could help sanitation workers clean up after the 3 million passengers that pass through Shinjuku Station every day.
A jingle-playing, googly-eyed team of trash-collecting robots are vying to make the world’s busiest rail station a bit cleaner.

East Japan Railway Company ( referred to as JR East ), which runs several lines in Tokyo’s bustling Shinjuku Station, recently wrapped up a roughly 10-week trial of these eye-catching robots. The machines stand just over three feet tall, and roll autonomously along preprogrammed routes through the station’s underground concourses between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. Once full, they trundle back to the station’s garbage collection area on their own.

Each of the three robots sports a different color (green, yellow, or red) to match their accompanying rail line. They definitely don’t look like your average sad, overflowing waste bin. Instead, they stroll up to commuters with bright lights and a front-facing screen showing cartoon eyes . Music appears to play when trash gets fed into them. An accompanying illustration of Shinjukuma , the station’s bear mascot, shows passengers which bins are for general trash and which are for plastic bottles. It’s all very Japanese.

JR East officials are hoping these bins on wheels will help relieve some of the burden on garbage collectors who struggle to keep up with trash generated by the millions of people passing through every day. The station, which sits on the western edge of central Tokyo, sees nearly three million daily passengers, an absurd amount of foot traffic that earned it a Guinness World Record . But more people means more trash. According to Tokyo Weekender, sanitation workers in the station unload garbage from fixed bags more than 10 times per day.

The robots could help, but only if they don’t get in the way and create more problems than they solve. Though JR East reportedly tested out a pair of garbage robots back in 2023, that was in a much smaller station and only for three days. Shinjuku is a much bigger challenge and serves as a kind of stress test to see if they are able to operate safely and effectively in densely packed areas.
Robot cleaners are here to stay

Tokyo isn’t the only city experimenting with trash robots. A cat-themed, mobile trash unit made a brief appearance in Paris’ Charles De Gaulle airport last year. In Singapore, an autonomous robot started collecting garbage in 2019 at Jewel Changi Airport , the shopping complex attached to the city’s main airport. And while trash collection is still relatively niche, automated cleaning robots are quickly becoming mainstays in many modern transportation hubs. Houston , Baltimore , Pittsburgh , and Oakland are among the many cities in the United States already putting robot cleaners to work scrubbing and mopping airport floors.

Making these robots seem cute isn’t just for attracting selfies. It’s also a self-defense strategy. Humans have a mixed track record when it comes to sharing space with robots. In 2024, the New York Police Department retired a 400-pound, egg-shaped surveillance robot from patrolling subway lines after facing pushback from privacy activists and concerned citizens, some of whom felt uncomfortable near the lifeless, imposing monitor. Years earlier, a friendly hitchhiking robot called HitchBot made it about two weeks into its trip across the United States when it was found vandalized and beheaded in Philadelphia .

Could cartoon eyes and a cute mascot have saved those robots? It’s difficult to say, but at least the Tokyo garbage robots seemed to make it through their trial without any dissected parts. That’s an improvement.

Many B-25 bombers are preserved in museums, but a handful of them actually remain flightworthy today.

One of those flight-ready B25s is a plane nicknamed Show Me . The aircraft belongs to the Missouri Wing of the Commemorative Air Force, and has taken to the sky every fall since 2009 to demonstrate its impressive aerial bombardment capabilities. But Show Me doesn’t unleash an arsenal of destruction anymore. Instead, the B25 releases a bevy of hollowed-out pumpkins filled with red, white, and blue pool chalk. However, aircraft recently dropped more than gourds for onlookers outside St. Louis. During this year’s flight, Show Me also deployed a pumpkin stuffed with the ashes of the Missouri Wing’s late, beloved volunteer, Lou Tacchi, Jr.
“His family was all on board with it,” current wing commander and retired pilot Rob Jenner told St. Louis public radio . “They had shirts printed up, and they called it the ‘Pop Drop.’”

Some of Tacchi, Jr.’s ashes were also packed away inside four .50-caliber shells that will now remain aboard the B-25. According to Jenner, their departed colleague will “fly with us forever,” thanks to his final request.

How Humans Are Helping Golden Jackals Conquer Europe
By unintentionally protecting jackals from larger predators, people are aiding in the expansion of a remarkably adaptable canid.

The golden jackal isn’t always the color of gold; its coat ranges from creamy beige to a rusty brown with black striations. It is, however, living in a golden age—thanks in part to the ubiquity of humans.

Native to Eurasia, golden jackals in Europe have historically been confined to the southeastern tips of the continent, mainly the Balkan countries. Over the past century, though, Canis aureus has slowly started colonizing new areas of Europe, with a steep acceleration over the past two decades. Golden jackals are expanding their range, reaching as far west as Spain and as far north as the Arctic. Scientists say the expansion represents one of the most dramatic changes in the range of a species in today’s world. New research, including genetic analysis, is revealing what’s driving the jackal’s spread and the part people play in the animal’s success.

One factor that has contributed to golden jackals’ expansion is anthropogenic climate change, which has decreased snow cover and probably revealed more suitable canid habitat. The habitat fragmentation that comes with farming and urbanization is another likely influence, since golden jackals prefer a patchy environment. The species also adapts readily to human-altered landscapes and can disperse hundreds of kilometers in search of new habitat. And, not least of all, researchers suspect that humans cleared the way for them by extirpating wolves across much of Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries.
“The fact that they did not have any competitor made it easier,” says Jennifer Hatlauf, a wildlife ecologist who manages the Golden Jackal Project in Austria .

Today, researchers estimate that around 150,000 golden jackals inhabit 23 European countries, populating a range that’s 46 percent bigger than it was in 2016 . But wolf populations are growing, too; Europe hosts roughly 23,000 wolves today, compared to an estimated 12,000 as recently as 2012.

To better understand how humans, a growing wolf population, and the expanding golden jackal population interact, Hatlauf and a large team of researchers collected and analyzed data on the presence of golden jackals from all around Europe between 2001 and 2017. The information mainly came from playback surveys: Researchers played a jackal call from a speaker and listened for the response of real jackals, identifying the presence of individuals. The team then paired this data with data on wolf and human presence.

Their recently published analysis shows that the presence of wolves is the main factor limiting the expansion of jackals—a result that strengthens the hypothesis that the decline of wolves in past centuries likely opened the door to the jackal expansion. The team also found that human settlements create a shield that deters wolves and offers a refuge for jackals.

The “human shield” hypothesis isn’t new. Researchers have long known that prey or smaller predators take advantage of human presence to escape large predators. For example, some bear mothers with cubs find refuge from adult male bears by moving close to human settlements, especially during the mating season, when the males would try to kill offspring. Prey animals, such as wild turkeys, also seem to find safety near human-inhabited areas.

In places where wolves are absent, the data shows, jackals tend to stay away from humans, likely to avoid deadly encounters with our species. But where wolves are rooted in the landscape, jackals remain within humans’ proximity. “The jackal is three times smaller, so there’s simply no chance for a jackal if you have a core area of wolf populations,” says Hatlauf. That same life strategy is probably going to apply in other areas that jackals will reach in the future as they expand even farther, she adds.

“The work is excellent,” says Luigi Boitani, chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Large Carnivore Initiative for Europe, who wasn’t involved in the research. The idea that the wolf’s extirpation played a role in the jackal’s expansion and that human presence shapes the relationship between the two species has long crossed scientists’ minds, Boitani says, but no one was able to prove it with actual data until now.
